# 20. Monitoring & Observability

<!-- Generated by tools/build_checklists.py. Edit the generator to change checklist structure. -->

**Purpose:** Keep a static site observable after launch using free or open-source-friendly checks for uptime, performance, errors, and content integrity.

## Universal Constraints
- [ ] The solution must remain static front-end only: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, documents, and generated static files only.
- [ ] The stack must avoid proprietary lock-in, paid builders, paid plugins, closed hosting features that cannot be replaced, and opaque third-party scripts where an open or free-tier-friendly alternative exists.
- [ ] Every decision must be documented as a quality rule, acceptance criterion, or exception with rationale; implementation notes belong outside the checklist.
- [ ] Every checklist item must be testable by review, automated audit, source inspection, browser testing, or client sign-off.
- [ ] Manual exceptions must record the owner, reason, expiration date, affected pages, and residual risk.

## Must Exist
- [ ] An uptime monitoring plan using free-tier-friendly tools or self-hosted checks where appropriate.
- [ ] A production smoke test list for homepage, contact page, forms, key services, sitemap, robots, and 404 page.
- [ ] A performance monitoring cadence using free lab checks and field data where available.
- [ ] A search visibility monitoring cadence for indexing, sitemap, robots, and major metadata issues.
- [ ] A form delivery monitoring process using test submissions and provider dashboards.
- [ ] A broken-link monitoring process for internal and important external links.
- [ ] A JavaScript error monitoring policy that avoids collecting personal data and does not require paid tooling.
- [ ] An incident response note with owner, escalation channel, rollback path, and expected response time.

## Must Be True
- [ ] Monitoring must check the deployed production URL, not only the repository.
- [ ] Alerts must go to someone responsible for action.
- [ ] Static-host incidents must include DNS, TLS, CDN, redirects, cache, deploy status, and domain expiry checks.
- [ ] Performance regressions must be treated as release quality issues, not only SEO concerns.
- [ ] Forms must be monitored end-to-end because static pages cannot store submissions.
- [ ] Client-visible changes must be logged after launch.
- [ ] Monitoring tools must not add heavy scripts to the site unless justified.
- [ ] Error logging must avoid capturing form contents or personal data.

## Must Be Checked
- [ ] Check uptime from at least one external location after launch.
- [ ] Check TLS certificate validity, HTTPS redirects, and mixed content.
- [ ] Check domain and DNS expiration dates.
- [ ] Check sitemap fetchability and robots accessibility.
- [ ] Check key pages with no-cache or fresh browser sessions after deploys.
- [ ] Check free Search Console or equivalent webmaster tooling where the client uses it.
- [ ] Check analytics for sudden traffic drops, conversion drops, 404 spikes, and unusual referral patterns.
- [ ] Check that alert noise is low enough that real incidents are not ignored.

## Must Be Avoided
- [ ] Avoid adding paid APM tools to a static brochure site without a clear need.
- [ ] Avoid relying on client complaints as the first monitoring signal.
- [ ] Avoid monitoring only homepage uptime while forms or key pages fail.
- [ ] Avoid logging user input, full URLs with personal data, or session replay by default.
- [ ] Avoid alerts with no owner or action path.
- [ ] Avoid ignoring domain, DNS, and certificate lifecycle risk.

## Premium Acceptance Standard
- [ ] Post-launch health must be observable without proprietary lock-in.
- [ ] Monitoring must cover the business-critical path, not only technical availability.
- [ ] Every alert must be actionable.
- [ ] Monthly review must connect site health to business outcomes.

## Automation Hooks
- [ ] Use static audit reports on a schedule through free CI where available.
- [ ] Use simple open-source uptime checks or provider free tiers when they meet privacy and reliability needs.

## Detailed Best-Practice Review Areas
- [ ] Monitoring protects uptime, forms/lead flow, SEO visibility, performance, accessibility, security, user trust, and maintenance decisions with free/open-source-friendly tools.
- [ ] Uptime, domain/DNS, HTTPS/SSL, hosting, deployment, repository, forms, analytics, conversions, SEO, sitemap/robots, broken links, 404s, performance, assets, JavaScript errors, accessibility, security, privacy/consent, content, visual/UI drift, user journeys, campaigns, multilingual, blog, portfolio, products, CMS export, alerting, reporting, documentation, schedule, red flags, and final approval are checked.
- [ ] Alerts cover site down, SSL failure, domain expiry, deployment failure, form failure, traffic/conversion drops, 404 spike, indexing issue, and security access change.
- [ ] Reports explain what changed, why it matters, fixes, action owners, and separate traffic from leads and clicks from conversions.

## Report Output Required
- [ ] Report every failed automated check with severity, checklist category, issue code, affected file or page, evidence, whether it is script-fixable, and how to fix it.
- [ ] Report every manual-only failure with reviewer, affected page or component, expected standard, actual behavior, recommended fix, owner, and target date.
- [ ] Separate launch blockers from quality improvements so critical static-site failures cannot be hidden by low-priority polish notes.
- [ ] Attach the JSON audit report, Markdown audit report, screenshots where visual proof is needed, and manual QA evidence for browser, device, keyboard, screen reader, form, analytics, and live deployment checks.

## Evidence Required
- [ ] Record reviewed pages, tools used, dates, reviewers, unresolved exceptions, and links to generated reports.
- [ ] Attach screenshots or source references for failures that cannot be proven by automated reports.
- [ ] Mark checklist items as complete only when the production static output satisfies the rule.
